prime_skills: Anderson's fastball shape is the whole argument for why Double-A hitters have looked overmatched. Twenty inches of induced vertical break on a four-seamer is elite in the majors, let alone against A-ball-to-Double-A bats seeing that kind of carry for the first time, and it produced the second-best whiff rate of any fastball in last year's entire draft class, trailing only Liam Doyle's. Forget the ERA entirely, that number tells you almost nothing about a college-polished arm skipping straight to Double-A, what matters is a 36.6 K-BB% and a 19.2% swinging-strike rate, both of which belong on a big league leaderboard, not a rookie-year pro debut. That production isn't just fastball-driven either, the slider and curveball are both generating called strikes at a rate suggesting advanced shape recognition from hitters seeing them for the first time, meaning he's not relying on one dominant pitch to survive an aggressive assignment. He’s been a revelation with a fantastic 2-plane slider, a nasty diving curve and an improved change up with some nice fade and a newly developed cutter.
ranking_explanation: I said last update Anderson needed to prove himself against actual competition before climbing further, and the response was less an answer than a rebuttal. He sits behind Made only because pitching prospects, even ones this polished, carry an inherent tail-risk hitters simply don't, one bad MRI and the whole profile changes overnight. Bats age gracefully into decline; arms sometimes don't get the chance to age at all.

comp: A Jose Fernandez and pre-Tommy-John Andrew Painter mash-up
prime_skills: Hernandez's fastball doesn't just touch elite velocity, it does so with shape that makes the top-of-the-zone version of the pitch nearly impossible to square up, ridiculous two-plane movement at 97 to 102 is a combination scouts rarely get to write about for a teenager. The changeup is the number that should actually worry rookie ball hitters more: a 43% whiff rate on a 63% strike rate is an absurd combination, most pitches that miss bats that often are also missing the zone that often, his doesn't. That's plus command on a swing-and-miss weapon, not just a swing-and-miss weapon, and it's backed up by excellent command grades on all three of his advanced offerings, not just raw shape. The curveball remains the one piece behind the other three, still needing real development, but a fastball-slider-changeup foundation this advanced already gives him a workable big league mix even before that fourth pitch catches up. I'm not going to cite an ERA here, rookie ball numbers mean almost nothing for a pitcher this talented, the swing-and-miss and command data on the individual pitches is the entire story.
ranking_explanation: Hernandez has a fastball that ramps from 97 to 102 with movement scouts describe as ridiculous rather than merely plus, and a changeup running a 43% whiff rate that might already be the best in the minors at any level. I wrote before he ever threw a professional pitch that Low-A hitters were simply out of luck, and nothing since has walked that back. He sits below Baez and Clark for the most unglamorous reason in prospect writing: he's a teenage pitcher, and teenage pitchers, however loaded the arsenal, are playing a game of inches against their own elbow ligament that hitters simply don't play. Proximity and health, not talent, are the entire gap here.

comp: Chris Carpenter-ish, with a slider instead of a curve
prime_skills: Sloan's fastball has added a full velocity grade since his pro debut, sitting 97 to 98 and touching 100 now against a 93-to-96 band he showed at signing, and it's paired with a 1/7 sweeper that's shown real curveball-caliber depth on top of its horizontal bite. What's worth flagging honestly is that his walk rate has climbed right alongside the added velo juice, meaning his K-BB% has actually come down a bit from his debut year even as the raw swing-and-miss numbers have held mostly steady, that's the profile of a pitcher whose stuff is outrunning his current feel for exactly where to locate it, not a decline in true command. He debuted at Low-A with just 15 walks in 82 innings, so the underlying feel for the strike zone is real, this looks like a temporary recalibration period as his velocity climbs rather than a lasting command regression. His changeup might be the best individual pitch in this whole system regardless of level, a personal catcher's on-the-record praise aside, the shape and the strike rate on it both grade out ahead of most upper-level arms, let alone a pitcher his age.  Sloan also throws a solid split changeup and an electric hard vertical slider/cutter with plus to plus, plus command of his stuff for his age.  The gyro slider and splitter play off each other very nicely, he’s a fun pitcher.
ranking_explanation: Sloan doesn't have gaudy strikeout totals to hang a ranking on, and that's fine, because the stuff grades out electric regardless of what the box score says on a given week: a mid-90s fastball with real ride, a sweeper with legitimate curveball depth, and command that's genuinely plus-to-plus-plus for a pitcher this age. The fastball has ticked up a full grade since his pro debut, and I'll flag the one real yellow flag in the file honestly, his walk rate has climbed alongside that added velocity, a 17.8 K-BB% this year against a 22.5% mark last season. That's the swing skill to watch the rest of the year. He's one of my personal favorite arms in this system, a safe bet for a great No. 2 starter for a long time, which is precisely why I don't rate him as a true ace type the way I do Hernandez or Sykora when healthy.

prime_skills: Sykora's three-level 2025 run before the injury is the kind of statistical trend that's almost impossible to find anywhere else in the minors, and I'd rather talk about the strikeout and whiff data than the ERA, which tells you almost nothing about a teenager blowing through three levels in one year. He ran a 44.4% whiff rate across that stretch, an absurd number for any pitcher at any level, generated primarily off a fastball that touches 100  with ridiculous extension that has more run that ride, a devastating mid-to-high-80s splitter and a mid 80s hard vertical slider. He led all of the minor leagues fStuff before the elbow gave out and has no timeline for a return this year at the moment.
ranking_explanation: This dude is a freak and could be the top prospect when he returns.  The closer we get to Sykora returning to the mound, the more he will move up in the rankings.  Ideally he will add some pitches to the arsenal before he hits the majors as well, he would benefit from a bridge pitch from the fastball to the slider.  Keep in mind, these guys returning from Tommy John generally have some rough command when they first get back and may lose spin, like Andrew Painter did on the fastball - so he might not return the exact same player.  We should assume at least 3-4 months in building back up and at the higher levels of the minors before a promotion to the bigs and the end of 2027 is more fitting to a 2028 Nationals contention window anyway.  Sykora has the ceiling of an ace and should be treated similarly to how Painter was when he went down, if not better.

comp: A Carlos Rodon arsenal grafted onto Nick Lodolo's mechanics
prime_skills: Watch White's release point before you watch the radar gun. He works from an under-three-quarters slot, not quite sidearm but close enough to create deception against same-side hitters, and that angle does as much work as the actual stuff. He simplified his breaking-ball mix this year rather than expanding it, he shelved the gyro slider he leaned on in 2025 and returned to his original slurve-shaped slider paired against a true sweeper, and that pitch has quietly become his second-best offering behind the changeup. He debuted a splitter this year too, only eight pitches thrown so far, flashing real swing-and-miss but too erratic to trust yet, and a single cutter attempt got hit for a homer, which explains why he hasn't gone back to it. The fastball has lost roughly an inch of induced vertical break this year, and his command on it has slipped right alongside that shape change, a real, measurable regression worth tracking rather than a small-sample blip.
ranking_explanation: Anderson passed White this year on pure in-season dominance, and Hernandez passed him on a cleaner present command grade, even though White's pure stuff, five pitches with two grading plus, still tops both of theirs on paper. Snelling ranks above him too despite the injury, since Snelling's fastball still carries more induced ride even in a limited sample. White holds his spot over Rainer and Culpepper below him purely on swing-and-miss upside, neither of those bats projects to be a difference-maker at the plate the way a healthy version of this arsenal projects on the mound.

prime_skills: Snelling throws from a three-quarters slot that creates a nice tunnel between the fastball and slider, and he made a genuine pitch-mix change this year, promoting the sweeping curve into his primary breaker while the changeup ticked up from 86 to 88-89 mph. His fastball climbed from 93 last year to 95-97 this year, real measurable velocity growth rather than a one-start spike, and he added it while dotting the pitch to an over-60% strike rate, an unusual combination of new stuff and maintained command. He generated a swinging-strike rate that climbed into the 20% range this year, mostly off that sweeping curve, which averages around 83 mph. He made his major league debut this year, then needed an internal brace procedure on his elbow immediately after that first start.
ranking_explanation: Snelling ranks ahead of White above him specifically because his fastball carries more induced ride even in a shorter track record, and the mix change to a real breaking-ball weapon happened faster for him than for White. He drops behind both Anderson and Hernandez purely on the medical file, a 10-to-12-month recovery timeline erases any argument for ranking him ahead of healthy arms with comparable stuff.

prime_skills: Eyanson's fastball carries over 16 inches of induced vertical break at plus velocity, real growth from a pitch that graded below-average on stuff models before this year's velocity jump from 93 in college to 95-98 as a pro. The gyro slider is generating the bulk of his called-strikes-plus-whiffs total as the bridge pitch between the fastball and curve, and both breaking balls currently share a similar 12-to-6 vertical shape, leaving the arsenal light on true glove-side, horizontal movement against right-handed hitters specifically. His command has dipped some since a Double-A promotion, worth watching whether that's a normal adjustment period or the stuff simply outrunning his current feel, but he has been better since the trade and the real test will be the jump to AAA where many pitchers have struggled with getting feel for the Major League ball and smaller ABS zone at that level.
ranking_explanation: Eyanson ranks behind Gonzalez above him because a college arm with a still-developing fourth pitch carries more present risk than a switch-hit bat already flashing two-sided power this loud. Eyanson's already pitching at Double-A while Kilby is still building his first full professional sample after an injury interruption and while Kilby is on a similar proximity timeline to Gonzalez, he does not have the same raw power upside.

comp: A lighter Paul Skenes with worse command
prime_skills: Susana's final seven starts of last season are the actual scouting report worth trusting over the full-season averages, a 10.9% walk rate over that stretch, good for a 39.1 K-BB%, and an 0.81 ERA, a completely different pitcher than the erratic-command arm he'd been earlier in the year. The slider at 88 to 91 mph is legitimately his best pitch and was still improving as of his last outings, a power breaking ball that misses bats at an elite clip. The changeup is a true diving, death-ball shape with curveball-like depth rather than a standard fade pitch, giving him a fourth true weapon on top of a fastball that sits 100-102. He missed most of the year following a lat injury, but has made two appearances on the season hitting up to 103 on the radar gun.
ranking_explanation: Susana ranked only behind Travis Sykora in fStuff last season and his stuff graded out similarly electric to star pitcher, Chase Burns. This is a legitimate top-40-overall talent on pure arsenal grades and he had been making strides forward in command over a 6-7 start period similar to what I saw in Jacob Misiorowski before the became the Miz we know and love.

comp: Zack Wheeler-esk with some Garrett Crochet leg action
prime_skills: Flora led all of Division I with a 1.06 ERA this spring at UC Santa Barbara while setting the program's single-season strikeout record, and the pitch-level shape backs up why the results held against a full college slate rather than a few good starts. His fastball averaged 96.1 for the season with 17.6 to 20-plus inches of induced vertical break and a flat approach angle, a shape that makes the carry play up beyond what the raw velocity alone suggests. He throws two distinct sliders, a 78-81 mph sweeper with real horizontal depth and an 86-89 mph gyro-cutter shape, both flashing plus, giving him two different breaking-ball looks off similar arm speed rather than one shape thrown at two speeds. A developing kick-change with some nasty bite when it’s on rounds out a four-pitch mix that already graded as one of the most complete college arsenals in this draft class.
ranking_explanation: Flora ranks behind Susana purely on lack of total professional sample, zero innings pitched as a pro against Susana’s own real, if health-interrupted, track record. He ranks ahead of Gonzales below him because a four-pitch college arsenal this advanced already grades out safer than an unproven prep bat's raw power, even one with Gonzales' specific exit-velo ceiling.

prime_skills: Lagrange's stuff grades top-of-system regardless of level, a fastball that touches 103 from a 6’7” frame out of a higher three-quarters slot paired with a hard vertical slider that seems to disappear as it leaves his hand. His two-seamer, carrying real arm-side run, has been close to unhittable against left-handed batters specifically all year. The command swings tell the real story of his season though, a dramatic early-season improvement gave way to the same erratic Double-A command that dogged him a year ago, the exact same pattern repeating rather than a new problem emerging.  He’s been out since July after spending his last few appearances in June in the pen in an effort to likely prepare him to pitch out of the pen for the MLB club down the stretch and in the playoffs.
ranking_explanation: Lagrange ranks behind Gonzales above him purely on risk profile, a command-erratic power arm carries more variance than a young prep bat already showing advanced swing decisions. He ranks ahead of Fischer below him because his ceiling, a true frontline starter if the command ever stabilizes, tops anything a power-over-hit college corner bat like Fischer projects to provide.

prime_skills: Zazueta is a lanky near-side-armer with phenomenal command who ran a 23.8% K-BB rate over 67 innings at A ball last year and has already been promoted through High-A to Double-A. The Dodgers system is ridiculous right now, Zazueta specifically works a four-pitch mix from a weird arm slot with an elite reported negative 4.3 degree vertical approach angle on the fastball, extreme deception that gets hitters swinging under the heater constantly. Unlike Ryan, he throws a standard changeup against a splitter with excellent freezing fade and doesn't carry a curveball or sinker, though he might benefit from adding both eventually. The changeup is his primary secondary, and his slider carries a gyro, vertical-drop shape that freezes hitters and pairs beautifully off the low release point on the four-seamer. He rarely throws the sweeper, and it plays almost like a deep curveball given his arm angle. This week he struck out eight and walked none, allowing just one hit over five innings on 60 pitches in that first Double-A look.
ranking_explanation: Zazueta’s gap between his fScore and his public ranking is exactly the kind of value worth chasing in points and OBP formats where his command-first profile plays best. He ranks behind the more established arms like Flora and LaGrange in this tier.

prime_skills: Chourio's command at 17 and 18 years old should scare hitters more than his fastball shape does, just five walks in 51.1 innings last year is close to unheard of, and he's carried that into 2026, an 18-year-old whose 11 Low-A starts, a 4-0 record, 1.88 ERA and a 44-to-9 strikeout-to-walk ratio, forced Kansas City to bump him to High-A by mid-June. The two-plane curveball is his real weapon, thrown inside to right-handed hitters and down-and-away to lefties, and while the fastball carries only decent ride rather than elite shape, his ability to locate it consistently generates the results. He's added a traditional cutter and a sweeping slider to the mix this year, though the slider still lacks bite and the cutter earns more mishits than outright whiffs, both real additions to his three-pitch foundation rather than finished offerings yet.
ranking_explanation: Chourio's fScore ranks him as the safest teenage arm in this whole tier purely off command, and command grades this advanced at 17 and 18 are what separate a real developmental fast track from a projection arm hoping stuff eventually translates. He ranks ahead of Morales below him because a pitcher already forcing an aggressive High-A assignment at 18-years-old and carrying the command forward on feel alone carries a higher peak projection than a bat still needing to answer real hit-tool questions at the same level.

comp: A mini Zack Wheeler mechanically, with Ryan Helsley's relief-arm ceiling if it doesn't stick as a starter
prime_skills: Wood's fastball generates absurd swing-and-miss off beautiful induced vertical break from a low release point, elite carry paired with real arm-side run and command that already grades ahead of most college first-rounders. He's a shorter, athletically built arm who'd be a legitimate weapon in a bullpen role tomorrow, but his full starter's arsenal raises the ceiling well beyond that floor, a high-velocity power curve with real drop as his primary secondary. He's actively reshaping the rest of his mix too, he's gone on record saying the tight gyro slider he debuted with might get replaced, and in his first pro start he already showed a changeup and a two-plane slider flashing as a legitimately plus pitch, real in-season arsenal evolution rather than a finished, static mix.
ranking_explanation: Real industry chatter has Wood debuting in a Phillies bullpen role almost immediately given how advanced the fastball and curveball already play against professional hitters, and that proximity is exactly why his fScore outpaces several college arms with longer track records elsewhere in this tier. He ranks ahead of Scarborough below him purely on health, Wood has a full season of evidence behind him where Scarborough is working back from an illness that cost him most of 2026 and while Wood has reached pitch counts of 80 at this point in the year, the Phillies could use him as an elite weapon down the stretch for their playoff run in 2026 - they won’t want to regret missing out on this live arm in their hunt for a title as their hitting stars are aging.

comp: A Joe Ryan and Shohei Ohtani pitcher mash-up
prime_skills: Scarborough's fastball-slider combination carries the profile, a high-riding heater that tops out at triple digits paired with a diving mid-80s sweeper that breaks anywhere from a 1:30 to a 7:30 shape depending on which version he throws, real spin manipulation off the same grip rather than one pitch thrown two ways. His changeup targets left-handed hitters specifically, thrown to get them reaching outside the zone rather than as a show-me fourth pitch. He's logged just four complex-league innings this year after opening the season sick, a specific data gap rather than a talent concern, the stuff itself graded as some of the nastiest in the minors when healthy.
ranking_explanation: Scarborough's stock is almost entirely about missing 2026 to illness rather than performance, several names ranked ahead of him in this same system either graduated, got hurt worse, or simply underwhelmed to open the year, which is exactly how he's still sitting this high despite the lost time. I'd expect the fastball-slider combination to push him back up the list once we have more health, but he’s been on and off with a bunch of shorter starts this year, which makes me think he may be playing at well less than 100% health.

prime_skills: Pulling from my own draft coverage since Townsend wasn't part of the Memorial Day rankings. He’s a shorter build pitcher at 6’1 185 lbs and brings a deep five-pitch mix from an athletic, high three-quarters slot built heavily around spin, a fastball sitting 95-96 that touches 97-98 and rides well at the top of the zone, though it can get hit when left over the middle since it doesn't carry much lateral movement to bail him out. His mid-80s slider is a plus separator with heavy glove-side sweep, and his low-80s curveball is a true hammer, a traditional 12-to-6 shape that's flashed 3,000-plus RPM on TrackMan and locks up left-handed hitters specifically.  Townsend is evidently also going to lower his arm-slot (at least the plan the Cubs have for him) and he was already one of my favorite players overall in the draft class.  The only concern I have is the Cubs have been poor at pitcher development for a very long time - it’s hard to remember the last good strikeout pitcher that actually came out of their system.  Steele and Horton are effective, but don’t have upper rotation upside in stuff alone.
ranking_explanation: A draft-eligible sophomore with a five-pitch mix this deep already projects a higher peak season than several more experienced arms in this same tier, real diverse weapons against both platoons rather than a two-pitch profile leaning on one shape. He ranks behind Alvarez above him purely on zero professional innings pitched, not on stuff, which already grades out ahead of several more experienced names in this range.  Pitchers are inherently risky and I believe long-term Alvarez has very low risk based on his hit profile.

comp: A meld of a lighter Tarik Skubal and Sonny Gray
prime_skills: Doyle's fastball carries big-time ride at 98 mph from the left side, and his bulldog mound presence along with a high-effort, high-arm-speed delivery echoes Sonny Gray more than the raw stuff comp alone suggests. He's one of very few left-handed pitchers anywhere who features a real splitter, with a ton of dive that plays as a nasty off-balance pitch specifically against the fastball's shape. He added two new pitches this year, a revamped cutter with later break and a lower-velocity slurve that replaced his old curveball, and the result funnels fastball, cutter, sweeper and slurve from a similar look before the splitter breaks the opposite way to complete the deception.  Doyle’s command has been his biggest hangup, but it’s been much better the last four starts with a 31.3 K-BB% since late July and only a 10% walk rate (which is still at best average) and his pitch counts are still maxing out in the mid-80s as he’s been slowly building up throughout the year.
ranking_explanation: I flagged in an earlier write-up that Doyle's ultimate ceiling depends entirely on secondary development, and this year's arsenal expansion, two new pitches added mid-season that immediately started producing a genuine five-pitch tunnel, is exactly the kind of proactive refinement that pushes his fScore toward a frontline outcome rather than a mid-rotation floor. He ranks ahead of everyone else in this specific tier on pure ceiling, a healthy frontline lefty simply outprojects any bat still developing.  He’s riskier than most starters in this tier because I think he’s either a top of rotation starter or a closer, all based on harnessing command and health.  The ceiling is much higher than Karson Milbrandt, but the floor is also significantly lower.

prime_skills: Milbrandt is a righty out of the third round in 2022 for the Marlins who has struggled with command since being drafted, but he tends to put up real gems when everything comes together. He works an odd, whippy three-quarters delivery that needs real mechanical refinement, his arm slot seems to shift based on the pitch he's throwing, which has led to both command inconsistency and real tipping issues, but when he's on, the stuff plays. The fastball carries arm-side run, and paired against the gyro slider it's a big-time swing-and-miss weapon. His breakout this year traces specifically to a kick changeup that was rarely used before and has turned into a weapon out of nowhere. I don’t understand why he has stopped throwing that pitch in AAA, but he has been much worse without the change up in his tool belt.  I mentioned in a recent X post that Milbrandt has hit the Quinn Mathews wall at AAA (like many other starters like Jaxon Wiggins) where specifically fastball command is entirely lost as they transition to the major league ball and deal with learning the ABS strike zone.  This may take more time than originally predicted for him to work out as the command gains from earlier in the season look completely lost.
ranking_explanation: Many will probably drop Milbrandt significantly in their rankings based on the small sample size of poor AAA production and the lacking pitch level data we now have to stare at through the offseason, but Quinn Mathews figured it out and has bounced back with a strong season.  We have already seen Milbrandt work through control issues from last season and improve earlier in the year and with his track record of adjustments, I’m confident he can do it again.

prime_skills: Bremner works from a high-effort three-quarters slot built around a fastball-changeup combo that's already advanced enough to move quickly in an Angels org that tends to push arms fast. The changeup specifically is close to unfair, real airbender action that should be a dominant weapon at any level, and while the camera angles I've had access to haven't let me fully confirm the fastball's shape characteristics, there's clearly real running life to it even without hard IVB numbers in hand. I flagged in the offseason that public reports had him down as a single slider when the tape actually showed two distinct breaking balls, a sweeper I liked and a spike-shaped gyro slider I graded as only average, and the in-season data has since confirmed exactly that two-slider mix, worth noting when a read like that holds up. The breakers overall still need real refinement relative to the two elite pitches carrying the arsenal right now.
ranking_explanation: If Bremner fully develops the sweeper, this goes from a solid No. 3 starter profile to a potential front-line No. 1 or 2 arm, the fastball-changeup combo alone, as great as both pitches already are, isn't quite enough on its own to get him there. I wish I had cleaner pitch-level data to nail down the fastball shape with full confidence, but the results have been very good (not great), regardless.  Bremner dropped in my rankings more because other players have just shown higher potential and we have the new draft coming in more than for anything he has done wrong.

prime_skills: Marquez was part of the return San Francisco got from Philadelphia in the Luis Arraez deal, and the underlying swing-and-miss data explains why I'd have moved fast to acquire him too: a near-70% whiff rate on his elite changeup at Low-A, while his sinker (primary fastball) sits 94-96 and touches 98, and a cutter-slider hybrid at 88-90 that keeps hitters honest even though it grades below the changeup. He compiled a 24% swinging-strike rate between two Class A levels this year, an absurd number for a 20-year-old, and he was nearly unhittable at both Low-A and High-A before the trade, real, sustained dominance across a full-season sample rather than one hot look. Marquez is a dude I have been trying to get on this list for a while now, he’s had one of the most impressive seasons in the minor leagues this year, pitching from an athletic build and easy _ delivery, Marquez started the year in A ball and has since come up to high A.  Marquez has a nearly 50% groundball rate on the year and his sinker runs almost 10” arm-side against only 15-16” of IVB and while it has good command, it’s not a pitch that will get many swings and misses.  The changeup has fantastic late drop and features fade against the flat sinker; it gets a ton of guys swinging over the pitch.  His third pitch is a gyro slider with a ton of drop, it’s a very nice pitch that generated a 26% swinging strike rate in low A.  Marquez will need to develop another pitch or two to complete his arsenal… whether it be a true four seamer to throw guys off the sinker and/or a sweeper that I recommend to add some east / west movement to his repertoire, he’s not a complete pitcher but has the makings of a very good mid rotation arm.
ranking_explanation: Marquez projects as a mid-rotation arm with front-line potential and a legitimate case to rank ahead of some more famous prospect names given his age, fScores and health track record relative to arms who've already dealt with real injury history. I can’t get over the fact I had him compared to Logan Webb prior to the trade to the Giants and now he might get the chance to learn from the man himself this Spring.

comp: A Pablo Lopez and Tanner Bibee mash
prime_skills: Forret is a nasty kitchen-sink, off-tempo athletic righty rather than a pure power-velocity type, and he added real ticks to his fastball after a Tread program stint, now sitting 94-95 with nice ride on the four-seamer, paired with a sinker that throws hitters off balance with good running life. His best secondary is a nasty vertical sweeper, and he backs it with a gyro-slider, a a death-ball spiked curve, that was also a Tread development along with a kick changeup carrying more negative vertical movement than his traditional change, giving him two distinct offspeed looks rather than one shape at different speeds. He's a true craftsman on the mound, sequencing and pitch-shape manipulation over pure stuff, which is exactly why the underlying performance is so much better than his public profile: since July 20, he's running a 1.65 ERA, a 0.93 WHIP and a 16.7% swinging-strike rate, real, dominant, sustained results.
ranking_explanation: Forret might be one of the most underrated starters in the entire minor leagues, and part of why is he hasn't racked up the kind of eye-popping strikeout totals that generate helium, he's just steadily, consistently good every single time out, a pitcher's pitcher with a genuinely full arsenal and the feel to actually use it. He’s been one of the best starters in AAA this year as a 22-year-old, well below age to level and while he’s unlikely to be a top of rotation starter and lacks the ceiling of some other starters lower down on the list, Forret looks like a great bet to be a very solid #3 or #4 low volatility starter - like a better Michael McGreevy.

comp: A Nick Pivetta and Jose Soriano mish-mosh
prime_skills: Hagaman is a big, down-plane righty drafted in the fourth round out of West Virginia who worked as a college reliever and was stretched out as a starter last year.  He’s already undergone an internal brace procedure (so hopefully injuries are out of the way) and he throws from a three-quarters slot and generates real ride on a fastball that plays up in the zone, backed by a nasty 2-and-8 vertical gyro slider with serious break, and he's developed a new 85 mph curveball since arriving in Arizona that carries negative 10 vertical break, more of a diving sweeper in practice than a traditional curve shape. His command improved dramatically after returning from the elbow procedure, finishing last season with a 34.4% strikeout-minus-walk rate and a 1.21 ERA over his final four starts, evidence the stuff and the strikes can coexist. He had a rough start to 2026 for unspecified reasons that delayed his season debut, but he's been ramping up since the end of May and since June 24th has a 24% K-BB rate and 2.41 JA ERA with regular pitch counts into the 80s.
ranking_explanation: Hagaman has achieved the target I set in my last rankings of getting to higher pitch counts while maintaining health and command.  Hagaman rates out as a likely future higher end mid rotation starter with plenty of swing and miss in the arsenal.  Forret gets the nod over Hagaman for me purely based upon his proximity to the majors when they are both the same age.

prime_skills: King is an athletically built lefty with a plus, high-riding fastball paired with a plus sinker that runs well and locates for strikes consistently, and the two pitches tunnel together well enough to keep hitters off balance even without premium raw velocity. The slider isn't a high-velo weapon, but it carries nice sweeping movement across the zone, and the curveball plays almost like a slow, traditional slider with two-plane break at nearly a 10-to-4 shape, an 18.3% swinging-strike rate at Low-A backing up the shape's effectiveness even at modest velocity. I saw him in person catching the first Low-A start of his career last year, and the stuff has been there all season even as the command has been volatile start-to-start. He's still just 19, meaning added velocity is a reasonable projection as he physically matures, but he needs to start throwing the changeup for strikes specifically, right now it's an underrated pitch with real movement that he simply isn't locating enough.
ranking_explanation: King is a polished, advanced-feel lefty on the mound whose breaking-ball consistency needs to catch up to how well the fastball and sinker already tunnel together. He walks too many guys and at 93 innings this year he seems to be running out of gas as the last few starts have seen a decline in pitch count and an increase in walks.  I see King as a mid-rotation arm and I don’t tab the upside others have on him as he lacks an elite out-pitch and struggles with consistent command.

prime_skills: Lin hit my radar really early in 2025, his first pro season where he posted a 2.08 JA ERA that got him to Double-A as a 19-year-old, a rare feat for an international arm from the Far East to move this fast. The fastball carries 18 inches of induced vertical break with plus ride, and it darts in against a fairly nasty 87-89 mph sweeper, a slower, loopier two-plane knuckle-curve, and a solid changeup, four distinct shapes for a pitcher this age. He's a slight build at 6-2, only about 180 pounds, but command is what separates him, just a 5.5% walk rate, precision locating rather than simply avoiding the zone. His fStuff model graded near 120 last year and has come down some in 2026, though that's mostly a competition effect as he's faced older, more advanced Double-A hitters and even made it to AAA prior to needing Tommy John surgery mid-way through the season, his swinging-strike rate has dipped from 16.1% to 12.9% specifically against the tougher level rather than any decline in his own stuff; keeping in mind the AAA ball is different than the ball at the lower levels.
ranking_explanation: We don't have the pitch-level Trackman data I'd like on Lin specifically, but he was thoroughly outclassing Double-A as a 20-year-old before a quad injury slowed him down and then subsequently needed Tommy John. The Athletics have had a rough time developing pitchers organizationally, a specific, tangible risk worth flagging rather than ignoring, but the underlying stuff and command combination here is good enough to overcome shakier player development if it holds.  He may not return to game action until 2028.

comp: A Jacob Misiorowski arsenal coming out of a righty CC Sabathia delivery
prime_skills: I still can't believe Sime lasted until the fourth round last year. My first live look at him in the Spring Breakout game was enough to get me on board immediately. He's built like a brick house at 6-4, 235, and the fastball is absurd, up to 102 mph, and he blew it past both Tai Peete and JJ Wetherholt in that same exhibition. The curveball is a clean traditional 11-to-5 shape, and the slider is a sweeping gyro pitch that plays more like a high-velocity vertical sweeper than a conventional breaking ball, a strange, hard-to-categorize shape, which is exactly why it's so tough to square up. Body-type-wise he almost reminds me of Alfredo Duno, but as a pitcher instead of a catcher, that same physically imposing, hard-to-miss presence on the mound.
ranking_explanation: Sime's command is inconsistent from start to start, but a near 42% strikeout rate is absurd enough that the ceiling stays sky high regardless. He needs to develop something with more horizontal movement between the changeup and a true fourth pitch and find steadier command, or this profile settles as a high-leverage reliever rather than a full-time starter, the raw stuff alone would play in either role.

prime_skills: Mathews is a big lefty with some ridiculous breakers that play way better when he can spin his fastball with mid-90s velo and above average rise to it and the slider is a swing and miss machine paired with that fastball.  His command has gone from elite to lost since 2024.  Mathews fell out of my Top 100 and my Top 150 this last update after not making any command gains y/o/y from 2025 after a phenomenal 2024. He has improved over the last three starts though with 23 strikeouts and only 5 walks and much better command of the fastball, change up and the sinker.  He still has #2 or #3 starter upside thanks to the elite slider and elite change up, but he needs to throw for strikes in order to get there.
ranking_explanation: Mathews projects as a mid-rotation arm who should provide a steady floor even in his rockier outings, the slider alone is a swing-and-miss weapon he can lean on when everything else is off. I'm including him here for completeness given he was squarely in this range entering the year, but this is closer to a graduation notice than an active prospect ranking at this point.

prime_skills: Doughty isn't a big guy, but he's got plus command and an advanced feel for spin that plays up well beyond his physical stature. The fastball has improved as he's added ride to it, helping it play up as a potential plus pitch, but the curveball is what actually makes this arsenal work, it might be the best curveball in the entire minor leagues, a 12-to-6 hammer spinning over 3,000 RPM. He throws from a more traditional high three-quarters slot and pairs it with a nasty two-plane hard sweeper with distinct separation from the curve, giving him a true one-two breaking-ball combination rather than one shape at two speeds. He throws the sinker low and the fastball high with excellent command of both, though the changeup still needs refinement to fully round out the mix, and he's been exceptional specifically since May 20th, building up to 80-plus pitch counts without any drop in stuff quality deep into starts.
ranking_explanation: Doughty has a legitimate No. 2 starter upside if the fastball shape keeps improving as he climbs levels, given how plus both breaking balls already grade and how well he tunnels the whole arsenal together. Developing the changeup to keep right-handed hitters honest is the last box left to check, everything else about the profile, command especially, is already ahead of schedule for a pitcher this age.

comp: A Yusei Kikuchi arm with some Chris Sale-esque arm action on the slider
prime_skills: Smith is a big, strong lefty with a quick, lower three-quarters arm action that almost snaps the fastball and slider in there at high-90s velocity, deception built into the delivery itself, not just the raw stuff. His biggest issue to date has been command, but a strong Arizona Fall League showing last year, 21 strikeouts against just six walks in 14 innings, offers hope that's trending the right direction. The splitter has good raw movement but poor command that limits its usefulness right now, and he's added a new cutter this year, learned specifically from Anthony Kay, that's already been excellent, a dated addition to the mix rather than a longstanding weapon. Walk rates remain high even though he now commands nearly every other pitch than the splitter reasonably well, which suggests the issue is more about attacking hitters early in counts than a mechanical repeatability problem.  He’s pitching out of the pen for the big league squad right now, which is probably a good move considering he has 10 strikeouts and 6 walks in his first 6 innings.
ranking_explanation: Smith has such outstanding raw stuff that command alone is putting his entire future in doubt, purely on stuff he could be an ace, but right now he profiles more like a young Blake Snell or Tyler Glasnow, electric shapes and velocities without the strike-throwing to match. Getting ahead in counts more consistently is the single swing skill that determines whether this becomes a frontline starter or an electric-but-erratic reliever.

prime_skills: Ryan is a strange name to see on a prospect list at all, he'll turn 28 in a few weeks, likely making him the oldest true prospect I've covered in years of doing this. He's got just four big league appearances but over a year of accrued service time thanks to a long injury history, and the carrying trait is that basically every pitch he throws grades out as plus, well-rounded stuff from a pitcher athletic enough to have shown legitimate starter-caliber command in his limited big league look. He was blocked significantly by the Dodgers' pitching depth despite performing well at Triple-A, and Detroit's willingness to take on his age and health history at the deadline tells you the industry still values the arm itself even with the unusual profile attached to it.
ranking_explanation: This is a unique asset-value case, a near-28-year-old with plus stuff across the board who Detroit will control through his age-31 season, less a traditional prospect and more a change-of-scenery buy-low bet on talent that's simply never gotten an opportunity. He rates outside of the top 100 mostly because of his age, if this guy was 22-years-old he would be a top 50 prospect just based on talent alone.

comp: A righty Framber Valdez, drop-and-drive delivery
prime_skills: Jordan signed well over slot as a fifth-rounder in 2024 to buy him away from a Florida State commitment, and the delivery is the story here, a drop-and-drive action out of a low three-quarters slot with a long, whippy arm action that creates a tough angle for hitters to pick up. The fastball isn't a pure velocity weapon, it's a lively, running sinker that projects as the foundation of a ground-ball-heavy starter profile, and his pro debut backed that up, a 2.36 ERA over 76.1 innings between the complex league and Low-A while pitching in both leagues' championship series openers. He's since seen the fastball climb from an amateur 92-93 sitting velocity to 92-96 with peaks touching 97.7 this spring, measurable growth since signing, and the ground-ball rate has followed the sinker's shape, a strong 1.52 GO/AO ratio that confirms the pitch is generating weak contact rather than empty swings. Jordan throws off this sinker with a gyro slider, a sweeper and a change up that all play to get groundballs.  He’s a 51% GB pitcher this year and one of the reasons I really like him is the ability to get ground balls and strikeouts simultaneously.  The gyro slider is a nice tight downer pitch that off the sinker gets guys swinging over it, similar to the change up which follows the sinker in movement and gets guys swinging on it early with a large velocity differential.  The sweeper has 15” of movement the other way against the sinker and is like a frisbee from his arm-angle. The change up has ridiculous fade.  He has really good stuff and is a guy we should all be keeping an eye on… this sinker first, deceptive arm-angle approach is having a ton of success against the high ride flyball, strikeout guys this year - an interesting trend to watch.
ranking_explanation: The command has climbed from a 40 grade as an amateur to a 50 as a pro after Anaheim's development staff emphasized strike-throwing in the California League, exactly the kind of improvement you want to see from a projectable, angle-over-velocity starter. He rates behind the more finished arms in this tier purely on distance from the majors, the mechanical foundation and the sinker shape both compare favorably to considerably more famous names.

prime_skills: Dzierwa is a monster, a second-round pick out of Michigan State best known for his size and stellar command despite that size. He's a college guy who's been a quick mover after a strong spring, and it's carried straight into a Big Ten Pitcher of the Year college resume, a 2.36 ERA with 104 strikeouts against just 22 walks, translating cleanly to pro ball. A weakness is he's only a three-pitch guy right now and profiles more as a back-end starter than a front-line arm in my opinion, a repertoire built around generating bad contact more than missing bats, leaning on a primary sinker rather than a four-seamer, backed by a plus changeup and fringy breaking stuff. He represented the Orioles in the All-Star Futures Game, considerable helium for a pitcher this new to pro ball, and he's shown plenty of toughness too, a bad-hop throw to the face backing up a play in May needed stitches above the eye and he was back on the mound six days later.
ranking_explanation: Between Frederick and Chesapeake he's now over 90 innings into his first full pro look with an ERA comfortably in the low twos, exactly the kind of quick, clean transition you want from an advanced college arm with feel like this. He continues rising up prospect rankings and is squarely on track for a 2027 debut, the lack of a true fourth weapon is the one thing keeping this from a higher spot on the list.

prime_skills: The stuff explains why Cleveland popped him early, a fastball that's a legitimate 60-grade pitch (or better) sitting mid-to-upper 90s that's topped out 100-101 with 20-plus inches of vertical ride from an interesting fairly over the top delivery. The slider is the true out-pitch, a 65-grade mid to high 80s breaker with sharp two-plane bite that ran a 51%-plus swing-and-miss rate in college, and he backs it with a 60-grade upper-70s curveball with heavy 12-to-6 spin and a developing 55-grade changeup that shows promise against left-handed hitters, four legitimate pitches for a college arm rather than the usual two-and-hope profile.
ranking_explanation: Four legitimate pitches for a college arm this advanced doesn't need a finished fifth weapon to profile as a frontline starter down the line. He sits in the middle of this tier purely on zero professional innings pitched, the pure stuff already compares favorably to several more experienced names ranked around him.

prime_skills: Eagen was one of the most consistent performers in the minors last year as a flier of a third-rounder in 2024, and he throws from the now-popular super-over-the-top arm slot shared by Yesavage, Tong, Gibson and a handful of the other breakout arms this cycle. He's got a nice four-pitch mix with an underrated mid-90s fastball carrying plenty of ride and some arm-side movement, a potential plus sweeping slider, and a plus diving 12-to-6 curveball, distinct weapons on both planes rather than one shape at multiple speeds. He's been better this year than the back-of-the-baseball-card numbers suggest, since May 5th he's run a 40% strikeout rate and a 1.64 JA ERA after a semi-rough April, and St. Louis acquired him from Arizona at the deadline alongside Sandro Santana in the Lars Nootbaar deal, telling evidence of how much the Cardinals value the recent surge. He dipped a bit in the industry rankings after that rough start thanks to the homer happy environment of Amarillo, but he was working specifically on refining the command on his split-change over the winter, and that focus is exactly what's paying off in the improved second-half numbers.
ranking_explanation: Eagen has been surpassed some by a couple of stronger pitching performances and a wave of breakout hitters elsewhere on this list, but I still see him as having a legitimate number two starter ceiling, more likely settling in as a solid number three given how the changeup lags the rest of the arsenal. Landing with a new organization at the deadline while trending upward is exactly the kind of storyline that tends to keep climbing rather than stalling out.

prime_skills: Arnold is an athletic lefty with a slighter build and throws from a unique arm angle that made him one of the top pitching prospects coming into the season and leaving the season, as he has a well-rounded fastball, slider, double change up combo and above average command, especially for the arm-slot.  The cutter is a gyro slider, more than a cut fastball, whereas he does throw a sinker for groundball outs against righties.  Arnold throws both a kick change and a split change in order to get both a downer arm-side movement profile vs. the glove-side fade of the kick change.  He’s had a rough first year of pro ball in general, however he’s been significantly better over his last five starts with a 30.5 K-BB% and 1.66 JA ERA even though he of course gave up two bombs in Amarillo a couple starts back.
ranking_explanation: Arnold is better than what we have seen for the majority of the year and the pitcher he’s been the last month or so is closer to who he can actually be, keeping in mind he’s going to have some tough PCL action next year to deal with and he will have a fairly rough home ballpark once he’s called up to the majors.

prime_skills: Russell is a huge righty out of Tennessee who had command issues in college slinging it out of a near-slide-arm slot, pitched half his time out of the bullpen, and was mostly a one-pitch fastball guy, but he's evolving into a full-time starter with startling stuff, an 16.3% swinging-strike rate and improved command, a 51% strike rate. The fastball has just okay vertical shape but carries considerable run, and the low arm slot creates unique deception hitters aren't used to seeing. He throws most of his secondary stuff off the fastball's shape, a sweeper that moves horizontally away from it and a gyro slider that tunnels vertically against it, built more for mishits than outright swing-and-miss, everything he throws lives up in the zone and works off tunneling the elevated fastball rather than burying pitches down and away.
ranking_explanation: There's meaningful reliever risk here since basically everything he throws lives up in the zone, and his off-fastball pitches simply won't play well down in the zone the way a more balanced arsenal would. He'd need to develop something for the bottom of the strike zone specifically to fully round out the profile, until then this reads as a distinct weapon in shorter bursts more than a true workhorse starter.

prime_skills: Command is the calling card, and the fastball backs it up, a 65-grade pitch sitting 95-97 that averages 96 and tops out at 100, thrown with a simple fingers-together grip that still gets heavy ride and deception up top. He mixes in a sinker to attack right-handed bats, an 86 mph cutter with heavy gyro spin off a spiked grip that works both sides of the plate, and an 82 mph slider with sharp top-spin that generates deep vertical drop, a four-pitch mix with command as good as advertised.
ranking_explanation: A four-pitch mix with command this advanced gives him a plausible chance to start rather than profile as a reliever, this isn't a thrower who happens to touch triple digits, it's a pitcher who repeats a simple, efficient delivery and locates to both sides of the plate. He sits in the back half of this tier purely on zero professional innings, the underlying command grades already compare favorably to more experienced names in this range.

prime_skills: Forbes started his college career as a shortstop before transitioning to full-time pitching in 2024 as a reliever, with 2025 being his first season as a starter, an uncommon developmental path for an arm with this much present stuff. He's got nasty stuff topping out at 100 mph from a funky, almost side-arm, quick-action slot out of an athletically built frame. The fastball-slider combination is nasty, the sweeper is a vertically breaking 12-to-6 shape rather than a traditional horizontal sweep, and the fastball, sitting 94-96, carries a fair amount of ride. The changeup is a solid pitch that gets left-handed hitters out fairly often, while the sinker has good arm-side movement but still lacks command.  He’s been in build-up all season and the Diamondbacks are being pretty conservative with his usage, but he’s been lights out with better command than I thought he would have out of the draft.
ranking_explanation: Forbes is a bit underrated if you only look at the back-of-the-baseball-card stats, it's easy to forget that Luis Castillo also had command concerns as a prospect before figuring it out at the big league level, and I've been around long enough to remember exactly how that story played out. He started this year on the injured list, worth factoring into any near-term timeline, but the stuff-over-results profile is exactly the type that tends to click all at once when the command finally arrives.

comp: A bigger Jose Berrios mashed with Kutter Crawford
prime_skills: Fajardo is a legitimately tough arm for hitters to square up, he gave up only one homer in his entire professional career until this year and made it to AA as a 19-year-old. I was a fan back when he was with Boston last year and like him considerably better than Jurrangelo Cijntje, the other arm the Cardinals landed from Seattle in the same general trade market. He throws a dirty kick-change that pairs beautifully against both the fastball and a vertical gyro slider, while a second fastball variant, more of a true two-seamer, plays up as a legitimate weapon specifically against lefties up in the zone thanks to late fade most hitters don't pick up in time. The gyro slider is filthy down in the zone, and he uses it as a true death pitch or spike offering against the kick-change, which fades hard in the opposite direction, distinct, deliberate shape variance rather than one breaking ball thrown at different speeds. He's currently running a striking 18% swinging-strike rate and a 34% CSW on the year way above age-to-level, with plus command as the velocity has ticked up alongside it and the 3.79 ERA is actually high considering his .366 BABIP on the year and the 2.49 JA ERA.
ranking_explanation: An 18% swinging-strike rate paired with command that's trending plus as the stuff ticks up is exactly the shape of a pitcher outperforming a fringy draft profile even with the increased homer rate against this year as he is pitching far above age-to-level in an organization packed mostly with college pitchers.  He has nasty breakers and the fastball plays better than the metrics suggest.  This kid is super underrated, but not by me.

comp: A MacKenzie Gore with a lower arm slot
prime_skills: McKenzie is a prep pitcher who got promoted to High-A after only one start at Low-A, and with just 26 professional innings on his ledger, he hasn't even qualified for a full fScore yet, this is pure stuff-and-projection right now, not a data-driven ranking. My buddy, Chris Blessing has said publicly he thinks McKenzie is the best pitcher in the entire Braves organization, and the pre-draft signing bonus said as much on its own. He works a low-90s fastball doing his best Chris Sale impression, slinging it from a low three-quarters, near-side-arm slot that's probably closer to Nick Lodolo's release in practice, the kind of low slot that should carry a distinct vertical approach angle advantage once someone tracks it. The curveball spins north of 3,000 RPM in a 10-to-5 shape and already looks like a potential double-plus pitch, and the changeup might be even nastier, a diving 12-to-6 offering that falls completely off the plate from that same low slot, tougher to pick up than the curve in the looks I've gotten so far. McKenzie has not pitched since June with a nerve issue in his left forearm, concerning, but only slightly long-term as we are still incredibly early in his developmental arc.
ranking_explanation: With only 26 pro innings banked, McKenzie's fScore hasn't caught up to how loud the raw stuff already looks, two potential double-plus pitches out of a deceptive low slot this early in a pro career is an uncommon combination. He ranks in this range purely on workload, not on any doubt about the arm, the Braves are building him up methodically rather than pushing him for results.  Fajardo has reached AA at the same age and is healthy - while he doesn't have as elite of secondaries as McKenzie, Fajardo gets the edge based on command, health, better proximity and a stronger performance record.

comp: Ranger Suárez if he sat 95-96 instead of 92-93
prime_skills: Hunter was a sixth-round afterthought a year ago out of Oklahoma State after two JUCO stops, and he's turned into the best swing-and-miss arm on the entire Orioles farm as a 22-year-old. His fastball has climbed from 90-93 at signing to 93-96 with a peak of 97 now, out of a three-quarters slot with a delivery that hides the ball behind his back before he comes forward, tangible deception that shows up in the results, hitters have managed just a .514 OPS against it with a single homer allowed all year. It's an odd blend too, scouts describe it as a low-spin, heavy fastball that still carries 19.3 inches of induced vertical break, meaning it looks like it should sink and instead rides through the top of the zone. The low-80s slider is his best swing-and-miss weapon against left-handed hitters specifically, a 36% whiff rate, and the changeup has developed fastest as a pro, low-80s with 8 to 10 mph of separation, gone from a show-me pitch to a legitimate weapon finishing right-handed hitters down and away.
ranking_explanation: Across two levels this year he's running a 13.9 K/9, the best strikeout rate of any pitcher in the entire Orioles farm system, ahead of far more decorated names like Boston Bateman and Joseph Dzierwa. Whether he ends up starting or relieving long-term is still an open question given the frame, but a 6th-round afterthought forcing the organization to reckon with him is exactly the kind of helium that tends to keep climbing rankings rather than plateauing.

prime_skills: Quick was a four-star offensive line recruit with legitimate SEC football offers who turned out to have incredibly nasty pitching stuff, he should have been a first-rounder, the raw arsenal plays well ahead of how it showed in the SEC in college, and he's been completely dominating both A-ball levels this year behind a nasty, high-arm-side sinker as his primary fastball, with a fantastic ground-ball rate and tangible swing-and-miss mixed in at Low-A. He already had Tommy John surgery back in 2024, so it's entirely likely his 2025 season came before he was fully back to strength, and now that he is, the results have followed, helped along by a Twins org that's demonstrably skilled at developing pitching even while their position-player prospects keep getting hurt. The four-seamer has high velocity but a fairly flat shape, while the gyro slider, more of a cutter really, is a beast, and the curveball is just a slower, loopier version of that same vertical gyro shape, keeping hitters off balance across multiple looks. He commands the sweeper and cutter well, but the changeup command still lags even though the shape plays nicely off the sinker.
ranking_explanation: A first-round talent who fell for signability and medical reasons is exactly the profile that tends to outperform its draft slot once the underlying health is fully behind him, and the ground-ball-heavy sinker foundation gives him a floor even before the changeup catches up to the rest of the mix. Minnesota's track record developing pitching is a distinct tailwind here, not just a hopeful footnote.

comp: Chase Burns light w/ some Joe Ryan mixed in
prime_skills: Kuhns stands deep down the mound with an athletic delivery and a low, 5.5-foot release point that creates a flat vertical approach angle hitters aren't used to seeing. The fastball is the premier weapon, an easy 60-grade pitch minimum sitting 93-96 and topping out 98-99, and the low release makes it play up with an outstanding 20 inches of carry that generates empty swings up top. The slider was the true development in his draft spring, a tighter, low-to-mid-80s breaker spinning 2,500-plus RPM that tunnels well off the heater, and the upper-70s curveball, a lethal 60-grade pitch with heavy 12-to-6 depth, actually took a backseat to the slider as the year went on, though it still tunnels beautifully off the elevated fastball.
ranking_explanation: Four weapons that all play off the same low release point is an uncommon foundation for a college arm this age, and it's exactly the kind of deceptive, deep mix that tends to miss bats even before physical maturation adds more raw velocity. He sits in the back half of this tier purely on zero professional innings, the underlying release-point deception compares favorably to more experienced names in this range.

comp: An Emmet Sheehan and Nolan McLean mash
prime_skills: At 6-2, Witherspoon isn't the biggest pitcher, but the fastball coming from a lower release point carries electric induced vertical break that plays well above what the raw velocity alone would suggest. The slider is a beast, a vertically cutting shape similar to Sheehan's, while the cutter carries its own insane vertical movement, more of a gyro slider in the mold of McLean's sweeper but with serious velocity behind the break, and the curveball is a slower, deeper shape than either. He's generating over 45% ground balls since joining Baltimore with a better than 17% swinging-strike rate, tangible swing-and-miss stuff even in a down year relative to his own draft-class peers, and he only walked 5.9% of hitters last year at Oklahoma, proof the underlying feel for the zone is there even though something's currently off with the mechanics and command as a pro. Baltimore acquired him at the deadline as part of the return for Adley Rutschman and while the walk rate was high in his first start in the Orioles organization, his last two starts have been a complete 180 turn on his otherwise downer of a year.
ranking_explanation: Witherspoon was one of my favorite arms from the 2025 class, he's got age on his side as one of the younger college pitchers in his group, and the arsenal itself is elite even in a rockier pro transition. He should develop into a legitimate number two or three starter with health, especially once he re-gains the command that made him such a coveted college arm in the first place.  Some will simply give up on him based on one rough year, but the stuff is great and it’s worth giving him a longer leash with his new organization.

comp: A raw McKenzie Gore with more wiry mechanics
prime_skills: Caminiti has an athletic build at 6-2, 195, with a mid-to-upper-90s fastball from the left side out of a fun, under-three-quarters arm slot, though the secondaries outside the sweeper have been inconsistent. The fastball carries natural ride and glove-side run since he almost slings it from that low slot, and the sweeper against lefties is legitimately amusing to watch, hitters flinch expecting to get hit and instead watch it land in the zone, though he still needs a different breaker specifically for right-handed hitters. He finished last season with a 2.75 JA ERA and was thoroughly dominant outside of two or three rough starts, building his pitch count into the 90s by year's end, and the changeup has since evolved into more of a splitter with distinct drop, a nasty change of pace off the fastball and slider that's continued improving into this year.  He’s run into some command issues this year and the stuff has not played well at AA as he needs to improve his pitch mix as guys have been getting more lift on him at the level.  Caminiti has a pretty solid strike-to-ball ratio, but he still ends up walking a fair amount of batters.  I think he needs to develop a gyro slider to bridge his arsenal between the fastball and his current breakers.
ranking_explanation: Caminiti showed marked improvement as last season progressed, especially the sweeper, which has become a legitimately dominant pitch rather than just a show-me weapon against lefties. Unlike some of the other young arms in this system, his pitch count kept climbing rather than plateauing, sound evidence of a durable delivery that should let him handle a full starter's workload as he climbs.

prime_skills: Franklin is another of the converted reliever types I love to gamble on when they have a couple elite pitches and when I saw him live at the Spring Breakout game he completely overshadowed Liam Doyle with three innings of excellence.  The fastball is an elite pitch with a ton of movement. He has a cutter aka gyro slider with diving movement that is good when located correctly and a nasty 12/6 sweeper that is his best secondary.  The sinker is an underrated pitch that I think is misread often with the primary fastball.  He sits closer to 98 than the 102 he tops at, but it’s in the tank.  The key for Franklin is going to be consistent command.  If he could refine the changeup or develop it into a splitter, he could be an elite front-line starter. He's dominated both sides of the plate this year too, holding right-handed hitters to a .222 average and lefties to just .143, though lefties have actually slugged a bit more against him, .286 to .278, a specific note that the extra-base damage he does allow skews toward same-side-opposite hitters even as the overall numbers stay excellent.
ranking_explanation: Franklin has actually performed better since being promoted to AA with an increased swinging strike rate and reduced walk rate, however the BABIP luck has been against him in his three starts at the level.  Franklin has been getting deeper up to mid 80s pitch counts in his last seven starts and has netted a 28% K-BB%, near 18% SwStr% and 1.95 JA ERA over that period of time.

prime_skills: Hill is a lean lefty who looks like a lefty George Kirby on the mound, and he throws a 95-97 mph sinker as his primary fastball, even though the four-seamer is arguably the better pitch on pure shape. The breakers are the story: an 81-84 mph slider is a two-plane sweeper netting a 14.9% swinging-strike rate on the year, the 82-85 mph kick changeup is generating a 19.3% swinging-strike rate, and the 11-to-5 curveball is generating a 21.6% mark and should honestly be thrown more often than it currently is. I saw his first professional start in person and posted a ton of video from behind the plate, and I initially thought Shane McClanahan watching the delivery, but the movement on the primary fastball is completely different, and on further review the profile actually tracks closer to a Max Fried type. Toronto acquired him from Minnesota at the deadline alongside Jhomnardo Reyes for Jeff Hoffman, telling evidence of how much helium this specific arm has built since his debut; however the Twins must be baffled by their inability to fix his command. The Blue Jays have since limited his pitch count as they attempt to correct mechanics and allow the stuff to play up - he has some crazy potential.
ranking_explanation: Hill has top-of-rotation-caliber stuff, and he should scrap leaning on the sinker so heavily in favor of the four-seamer and curveball, both of which grade out ahead of it on pure swinging-strike data. He'll have to harness the command the way the Miz eventually did, or he risks ending up a future Joe Boyle type, big stuff undermined by a command grade that never quite arrives.

comp: A Taj Bradley and Brayan Bello mash
prime_skills: Dishmey is a dude I've talked about a lot on the podcast since I saw him in low A last year and now he’s finally breaking into my to rankings, a lean, whippy-armed righty throwing from a lower three-quarters slot with plenty of ride on the fastball and an electric slider carrying quick-twitch mechanics and distinct arm-angle deception that help the whole arsenal play up. The fastball plays terrifically up in the zone, and while a lot of evaluators will point to his circle changeup as the best individual pitch, I'd frame him as a fastball, bullet slider and sweeper first, with the changeup rounding things out. In his final six starts of 2025 he ran 42 strikeouts against just six walks over 29.2 innings, and he carried that into 2026, electric outside of three rough starts. The fastball rides and runs, the gyro slider is a quick downer, and it all plays beautifully against a changeup that fades east, a slider that plays south, and a sweeper working west, three distinct horizontal directions off the same arm action.
ranking_explanation: A pitcher who gets better, not worse, on a level jump is exactly the profile that tends to keep climbing, and a six-inning no-hitter this deep into a full season is exactly the kind of data point that should push his fScore higher than a name still floating at this general range. He projects as a legitimate high strikeout middle of rotation option on pure arsenal depth, three distinct breaking and offspeed shapes working in three different directions off one arm action.  The Marlins are great at pitching development, which is one more notch in Dishmey’s case as he starts bumping up these rankings.

comp: Bryan Woo light mashed with some Dylan Cease
prime_skills: Murphy is a former first rounder with ridiculous fastball characteristics (up to 22” IVB on it.) and just returned from Tommy John.  The fastball runs into the lower/mid-90s with excellent ride to it and he’s good and pounding it into the top of the zone, but it does get nailed when he mislocates it.  He throws a curve against a 12/6 slider, it would be killer if he could add a sweeper to the arsenal or something with more horizontal movement and the change up has some splitter characteristics.  He’s a former top 100 prospect for me who had some troubles when first returning from injury, but had a nice run from late May until his call up.  Murphy started throwing a gyro slider this year and it’s become his second most thrown pitch, despite not having the best command.  It gets a decent amount of swinging strikes, but he hasn’t yet perfected the in zone command; while the traditional slider is still racking up over 20% swinging strike rates and has a 43.3% CSW, he needs to throw that pitch more - as for whatever reason he hasn’t thrown it in the last three starts even though it’s his best breaker.  He also started throwing a sinker this year and lackluster as a groundball pitch, only performing mediocre for whiff.
ranking_explanation: Given he's already pitched in the majors, this is really a graduation notice rather than an active prospect ranking, worth pulling entirely off future iterations of this list rather than holding a placeholder spot. I'm leaving him in this pass purely for closure on where the profile landed.

comp: A Cristopher Sanchez with an arm-side fastball
prime_skills: Mayfield had an excellent 2025 as the big lefty showed improved command from the middle of the season onward, including rising pitch counts and a striking 2.37 JA ERA on the year and followed it up with an even better 2026 prior to his recent injury. He's a big guy throwing from a tricky lower-three-quarters slot that gives the fastball distinct natural arm-side run, which trips up right-handed hitters, paired with a two-plane slider that's a bit slurvy, close to a sweeper if it carried more velocity, while the changeup freezes up left-handed hitters with tangible vertical drop and some air-bender qualities. He'd benefit from developing a bridge pitch or two off the fastball, a gyro slider or a downer curve specifically, to round out an otherwise two-pitch-heavy mix, and Detroit acquired him from San Diego at the deadline in the Casey Mize trade.  He hit the IL shortly after the trade and the IL or short stints for some of these traded prospect pitchers makes one think they may be tweaking some mechanics or trying to add a new pitch before getting them into game action.

comp: Michael King and Luis Castillo mash up
prime_skills: Smith was a third-rounder in 2023 out of high school and the Dodgers popped him at that spot even though he'd just had Tommy John surgery, telling evidence of how high evaluators were on the arm even hurt. He throws from a distinctly high one or two o'clock over-the-top slot and is known first and foremost as a fastball-changeup guy, and while we still don't have hard pitch-level Trackman data on him given how little the West Coast levels publish, the results speak for themselves, a five-pitch mix producing a 17% swinging-strike rate on the season and a strikeout-minus-walk rate near 30%. This is a legitimate breakout after 2025 was essentially a build-back-to-health season post-surgery. The fastball carries nice ride but also distinct arm-side run, giving it some sinker action rather than a pure four-seam shape, and the changeup is a diving pitch that falls completely off the table, legitimately one of the five best changeups in the entire minor leagues by shape alone. The slider has good velocity and tangible potential, though the cutter and curve are currently doing more of the swinging-strike work at this stage, the cutter holds solid velocity with average movement and works as a foil against the fastball's arm-side action, while the curve has good spin and should keep improving simply from more repetition. He's now with Detroit after being included as the underrated and “forgotten” piece in the Tarik Skubal trade, packaged alongside River Ryan and Zyhir Hope elsewhere on this list.
ranking_explanation: Smith has only made a couple of appearances after being acquired from the Dodgers and hit the IL out of the last one with an undisclosed injury.  These prospect pitcher injuries post-acquisition are a little sketchy and makes me think there is something more behind the story, as what are the odds all these pitchers traded outside of the pitchers the Orioles acquired at the deadline all end up on the IL.
